outline: Halogenoalkanes arise from ultraviolet radical substitution of alkanes, room-temperature electrophilic addition to alkenes, or alcohol substitution. Classify them by the number of carbon neighbours of the C–X carbon. Aqueous hydroxide, ethanolic cyanide and ethanolic ammonia give alcohols, nitriles and amines by nucleophilic substitution. Hot ethanolic hydroxide gives alkenes by elimination. $S_N2$ is concerted; $S_N1$ first forms a carbocation, stabilised by alkyl groups. Primary centres favour $S_N2$, tertiary centres $S_N1$, and secondary centres may use both. Weaker C–X bonds hydrolyse faster; aqueous silver nitrate in ethanol gives characteristic silver halide precipitates.

misconceptions.statement: Alkene addition of a halogen needs ultraviolet light.
misconceptions.refutation: Alkenes add halogens electrophilically at room temperature; UV light initiates alkane radical substitution.
misconceptions.contrast: Compare the starting hydrocarbon and conditions.

misconceptions.statement: Primary means the halogen is on carbon 1 of the longest chain.
misconceptions.refutation: Classification counts carbon atoms attached to the carbon bearing halogen, regardless of its locant.
Cyanide substitutes X through its carbon end to form a nitrile; ethanolic ammonia gives an amine.

misconceptions.statement: Aqueous and ethanolic hydroxide give the same main product.
misconceptions.refutation: Aqueous hydroxide favours substitution to an alcohol; hot ethanolic hydroxide favours elimination to an alkene.
misconceptions.contrast: Use solvent and temperature to choose the pathway.

misconceptions.statement: An SN2 reaction first forms a carbocation.
misconceptions.refutation: SN2 is one concerted step: nucleophile attack and C–X bond breaking occur together.
misconceptions.contrast: A free carbocation is the SN1 intermediate.

misconceptions.statement: Tertiary halogenoalkanes favour SN2 because their carbocations are stable.
misconceptions.refutation: Their crowded reaction centre hinders backside attack; alkyl groups stabilise a tertiary carbocation, favouring SN1.
misconceptions.contrast: Separate steric access from carbocation stability.

misconceptions.statement: A stronger C–X bond hydrolyses faster.
misconceptions.refutation: A weaker C–X bond breaks more readily: C–I faster than C–Br faster than C–Cl in comparable compounds.
misconceptions.contrast: Compare bond strength, not halogen electronegativity alone.

9701-15.1.1.motivate: One C–X product can be reached from an alkane, an alkene or an alcohol; choosing the route depends on the starting functional group.
9701-15.1.1.establish: Alkanes, exemplified by ethane, undergo free-radical substitution with $\ce{Cl2}$ or $\ce{Br2}$ under ultraviolet light. At room temperature, alkenes undergo electrophilic addition with $\ce{X2}$ to make a dihalogenoalkane, or with $\ce{HX(g)}$ to make a monohalogenoalkane. Alcohol OH can be substituted using $\ce{HX(g)}$; $\ce{KCl}$ and concentrated $\ce{H2SO4}$ or concentrated $\ce{H3PO4}$; $\ce{PCl3}$ with heat; $\ce{PCl5}$; or $\ce{SOCl2}$. State both reagent and condition when a route needs one.
9701-15.1.1.connect: The starting bond pattern predicts whether you substitute H, add across C=C, or replace OH.
9701-15.1.1.note:
- Alkane + $\ce{Cl2}$ or $\ce{Br2}$: UV radical substitution.
- Alkene + $\ce{X2}$ or $\ce{HX(g)}$: room-temperature electrophilic addition.
- Alcohol: substitute OH with HX, KCl/strong acid, $\ce{PCl3}$ and heat, $\ce{PCl5}$, or $\ce{SOCl2}$.
9701-15.1.1.self_explain: Which preparation route starts with a C=C bond, and what happens to that bond?

9701-15.1.2.motivate: The label primary, secondary or tertiary predicts how accessible the carbon bonded to halogen is.
9701-15.1.2.establish: Find the carbon directly bonded to X. Count how many other carbon atoms are directly bonded to that carbon: one means primary, two secondary, three tertiary. A methyl halide has zero and is considered separately. Do not classify from the halogen’s position number in the name.
9701-15.1.2.connect: This carbon-neighbour count helps predict which nucleophilic substitution mechanism is favoured.
9701-15.1.2.note:
- Primary: C–X carbon bonded to one carbon.
- Secondary: C–X carbon bonded to two carbons.
- Tertiary: C–X carbon bonded to three carbons.
9701-15.1.2.self_explain: Why is $\ce{CH3CHBrCH3}$ secondary although Br is on carbon 2?

9701-15.1.3.motivate: Replacing X gives several useful functional groups, and the solvent selects the chemistry.
9701-15.1.3.establish: Heat a halogenoalkane with $\ce{NaOH(aq)}$ for an alcohol. Heat with $\ce{KCN}$ dissolved in ethanol for a nitrile: $\ce{CN^-}$ attacks through carbon and adds one carbon to the chain. Heat with $\ce{NH3}$ in ethanol under pressure for an amine. To identify X, warm the compound with aqueous silver nitrate in ethanol. Hydrolysis releases halide ions, which give white $\ce{AgCl}$, cream $\ce{AgBr}$ or yellow $\ce{AgI}$ precipitate; bromoethane gives cream $\ce{AgBr}$. These are nucleophilic substitutions at the C–X carbon.
9701-15.1.3.connect: Compare this with hot ethanolic hydroxide, where removal of H and X forms an alkene.
9701-15.1.3.note:
- $\ce{NaOH(aq)}$ and heat: alcohol.
- Ethanolic $\ce{KCN}$ and heat: nitrile.
- Ethanolic $\ce{NH3}$, heat and pressure: amine.
- Aqueous $\ce{AgNO3}$ in ethanol: white/cream/yellow silver halide.
9701-15.1.3.self_explain: Why does ethanolic cyanide extend the carbon chain by one atom?

9701-15.1.4.motivate: The same hydroxide ion can produce an alkene when solvent and heat favour removal rather than replacement.
9701-15.1.4.establish: Heat a halogenoalkane with $\ce{NaOH}$ in ethanol. Hydroxide removes a hydrogen from a carbon adjacent to the C–X carbon while X leaves; the two carbons form a double bond. For bromoethane, $\ce{CH3CH2Br + OH^- -> CH2=CH2 + H2O + Br^-}$ gives ethene. An adjacent carbon must have a hydrogen for this elimination to occur.
9701-15.1.4.connect: Aqueous hydroxide instead gives an alcohol by nucleophilic substitution.
9701-15.1.4.note:
- Hot ethanolic $\ce{NaOH}$ favours elimination.
- Remove X and an adjacent H; form C=C.
- Bromoethane gives ethene.
9701-15.1.4.self_explain: Which atom must be present on a carbon next to C–Br for elimination?

9701-15.1.5.motivate: Mechanism questions ask when the new bond forms relative to C–X cleavage.
9701-15.1.5.establish: In $S_N2$, a nucleophile donates a lone pair to the C–X carbon while the C–X bond breaks in one concerted step; there is no free carbocation. In $S_N1$, C–X first breaks heterolytically, producing a carbocation and halide; then the nucleophile attacks the carbocation. Alkyl groups donate electron density by a positive inductive effect, stabilising the positive carbon. Thus a tertiary carbocation is more stable than a secondary, which is more stable than a primary carbocation.
9701-15.1.5.connect: The same alkyl groups also crowd the carbon and make backside $S_N2$ attack harder.
9701-15.1.5.note:
- $S_N2$: one concerted attack and bond cleavage.
- $S_N1$: C–X cleavage, carbocation, then attack.
- Alkyl positive inductive effect stabilises carbocations.
9701-15.1.5.self_explain: Why must an $S_N2$ mechanism omit a carbocation intermediate?

9701-15.1.6.motivate: Classification predicts a useful tendency, though secondary compounds can follow more than one path.
9701-15.1.6.establish: Primary halogenoalkanes tend to react by $S_N2$: their C–X carbon is accessible and a primary carbocation is relatively unstable. Tertiary halogenoalkanes tend to react by $S_N1$: three alkyl groups hinder backside attack while their positive inductive effects stabilise the tertiary carbocation. Secondary halogenoalkanes can react by a mixture of $S_N1$ and $S_N2$, depending on structure. These are tendencies for nucleophilic substitution, not a claim that every reagent forces substitution.
9701-15.1.6.connect: Check for elimination separately when the reagent is hot ethanolic hydroxide.
9701-15.1.6.note:
- Primary tends to $S_N2$.
- Tertiary tends to $S_N1$.
- Secondary can use a mixture, depending on structure.
9701-15.1.6.self_explain: Why do three alkyl groups make $S_N1$ more favourable than $S_N2$?

9701-15.1.7.motivate: A silver nitrate test can reveal both the halogen identity and how readily its C–X bond hydrolyses.
9701-15.1.7.establish: For comparable halogenoalkanes, C–Cl is stronger than C–Br, which is stronger than C–I. The weaker C–X bond breaks more readily, so iodoalkanes generally hydrolyse faster than bromoalkanes, then chloroalkanes. Warm with aqueous $\ce{AgNO3}$ in ethanol: hydrolysis releases $\ce{X^-}$, which precipitates with $\ce{Ag^+}$. $\ce{AgCl}$ is white, $\ce{AgBr}$ cream and $\ce{AgI}$ yellow. An earlier precipitate indicates faster hydrolysis under comparable conditions.
9701-15.1.7.connect: Mechanism preference also depends on primary, secondary or tertiary structure, so compare bond strengths using similar carbon skeletons.
9701-15.1.7.note:
- Bond strength: C–Cl > C–Br > C–I.
- Hydrolysis rate: iodo > bromo > chloro for comparable compounds.
- $\ce{AgCl}$ white, $\ce{AgBr}$ cream, $\ce{AgI}$ yellow.
9701-15.1.7.self_explain: Why does bromoethane form its silver halide precipitate sooner than chloroethane?
